title: Should your restaurant use a phone tree?
seoTitle: Restaurant IVR phone tree: yes or no? | ROAL
description: A restaurant IVR phone tree can help, but it can also slow callers down. Compare the tradeoffs, scripts, and simpler options before you decide.
question: Should my restaurant use an IVR phone tree, or is there a better way to handle calls?
answer: For most independent restaurants, a full restaurant IVR phone tree is usually too much friction. Keep it simple unless you truly need to route callers to separate departments, because many callers just want hours, a pickup order, or a person who can help fast. A short greeting plus direct call handling is often the better fit.
summary: You’ll learn when a phone tree helps, when it hurts, and how to set up a simpler phone setup that fits a restaurant.
intro:
A restaurant IVR phone tree is usually a no for small and mid-size spots. It can help in a few special cases, but most callers want one thing fast: place an order, ask hours, or speak to staff.

If your menu changes often, your team is small, or you get a lot of rush calls, extra menu layers can slow people down. A simpler setup often works better: one greeting, one number, and clear routing for the few calls that really need it.

sections.h2: What is a restaurant IVR phone tree, really?
sections.body:
A restaurant IVR phone tree is the “press 1 for this, press 2 for that” menu people hear when they call. It can send callers to different places, like pickup orders, reservations, or voicemail. In a restaurant, that sounds organized, but it can also feel like a barrier.

For a takeout shop, the caller often wants the fastest path to a real answer. A good test is this: can the caller do the most common task in one step or two? If not, the tree may be making the phone harder to use, not easier.

Use this as a quick check:
- Do callers mostly ask about hours, address, parking, or the menu?
- Do they mostly want to place pickup orders?
- Do you have separate staff for reservations, catering, or parties?
- Can your team keep the menu tree updated every time hours or specials change?

If the answer is mostly no, a long IVR is probably not worth it.

sections.h2: When does a phone tree make sense for a restaurant?
sections.body:
A phone tree can make sense when the call types are truly different and the routing saves time. For example, a family restaurant might want one path for reservations and another for takeout. A larger place may also want a separate line for catering or a manager.

Here’s a simple version that still respects the caller’s time:

1. “Press 1 to place a pickup order.”
2. “Press 2 for hours, address, or menu questions.”
3. “Press 3 for catering or private events.”
4. “Press 4 to speak with staff about a concern.”

That’s enough for many restaurants. Do not stack three more menus after that. The more layers you add, the more people hang up.

A useful rule: if your staff can answer the same question in under 20 seconds, the IVR should not make the caller repeat it twice.

sections.h2: When does a phone tree get in the way?
sections.body:
A phone tree gets in the way when the caller already knows what they want. That is common in restaurants. Most people call with a short task and a short attention span. If they have to listen to a list, wait for a prompt, and then get bounced to voicemail, you may lose the order.

Bad fit examples:
- A pizza shop with one main number and one small team.
- A deli that gets lots of fast lunch calls.
- A takeout spot that changes its menu often.
- A family restaurant that needs the phone answered during rush.

A better script is often just this: “Thanks for calling. I can help with pickup orders, hours, menu questions, and reservations.”

If you use call forwarding, keep the setup simple. Many carriers use codes like *72 to forward all calls and *73 to turn it off on some landlines, while some mobile carriers use different codes. Always confirm with your carrier and test with a real call. For a quick reference, see [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes) and [how to test that call forwarding works](/blog/test-call-forwarding).

sections.h2: What does a better phone setup look like for a small restaurant?
sections.body:
For many owners, a better setup is not a tree. It is a clear greeting, good forwarding, and a fast way to capture the call. ROAL does this by answering the restaurant’s phone, taking pickup and delivery orders from the live menu, and sending a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

A simple setup can look like this:

| Part | What to do |
|---|---|
| Greeting | Keep it short and friendly |
| Routing | Send pickup, questions, and reservations to the same place unless you truly need separate paths |
| Forwarding | Forward the existing number only when busy or unanswered, or all calls if needed |
| Follow-up | Put tricky calls in a staff inbox with a summary |

A workable greeting line: “Thanks for calling Tony’s Deli. I can help with pickup orders, hours, address, parking, and menu questions.”

If you are comparing phone tree logic to a simpler phone host, it can help to read [AI phone host vs a press-1 phone menu](/compare/phone-menu-ivr) and [phone greeting templates](/tools/phone-greeting-templates).

sections.h2: How should I decide yes or no for my restaurant?
sections.body:
Use this quick decision list. If most of these are true, say no to a full IVR and keep it simpler:

- You have one location.
- Most calls are pickup orders or basic questions.
- Your menu changes often.
- You are short-staffed.
- You do not have a person dedicated to managing phone menus.

Say yes to a limited phone tree if you truly need separate paths for reservations, catering, or private events. Even then, keep it short.

Think in numbers. Say your average pickup order is $28. If 10 calls a week hang up because the phone setup is annoying, that is $280 in weekly order value you might put at risk. Plug in your own average check and call volume to see what a missed or delayed call could mean for your shop.

If you want a cleaner model, ROAL can answer, quote a ready time, take the order, and hand other calls to staff with context. It also speaks the caller’s language and remembers answers you have already provided in the inbox.

sections.h2: How do I set this up without making the phone worse?
sections.body:
Start with the simplest setup that protects the phone. The goal is not to impress callers with a menu. The goal is to get the right call to the right place fast.

Try this setup order:

1. List your top 5 call types: pickup, delivery, hours, menu questions, reservations.
2. Decide which ones really need a separate route.
3. Write one short greeting and one backup message.
4. Set forwarding on your existing number, then test it from a cell phone.
5. Place tricky calls in a staff inbox with a summary instead of forcing a long menu.

For owners who want to test a cleaner approach, ROAL is set up by pasting the restaurant website, Google Maps link, or “Name, City” at /try. It reads public pages and menu files, builds a phone host in about a minute, and you can test-call it in the browser before you go live.

If you decide to go live, the restaurant keeps its own number and forwarding can be turned off any time.

takeaways: A full restaurant IVR phone tree is often too much friction for small restaurants.
Use a short menu only when you truly need to route different call types.
Test forwarding with a real call before you rely on it during service.
A simpler phone setup can protect orders without making callers repeat themselves.

faq.q: Do restaurants need an IVR phone tree?
faq.a: Not always. Many independent restaurants do better with a short greeting and a simple call flow instead of a long press-1 menu. If most callers want pickup orders, hours, or a quick menu question, fewer steps usually work better.

faq.q: What should a restaurant phone tree include?
faq.a: If you use one, keep it short. The usual useful options are pickup orders, hours and menu questions, reservations, and catering or manager requests. Avoid deep menus with multiple submenus, since that often slows callers down.

faq.q: How do I forward my restaurant number without losing it?
faq.a: You can keep your existing number and forward it to another line. Many landlines and some carriers use *72 to turn on forwarding and *73 to turn it off, but codes vary by carrier and plan. Confirm with your carrier and test with a real call.

faq.a: In many cases, yes. ROAL answers the phone, takes pickup and delivery orders from the live menu, answers common questions, and sends clean tickets to the kitchen screen. It also hands tougher calls to staff with a summary instead of forcing callers through a long menu.
